title: Efficacy and safety with aumolertinib plus anlotinib for untreated EGFR-mutant NSCLC with brain metastases
author: Jing Chen; Yin Pan; Meichen Li; Hui Yu; Baishen Zhang; Mingjie Yu; Xue Hou; Likun Chen
text:
Abstract
The efficacy and prognosis of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with brain metastases (BMs) are poor. The third-generation EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitor proved to have better intracranial efficacy, which combined with anti-angiogenic drugs can further improve the efficacy. We conducted a single-arm, phase 2 clinical study (GASTO-1063) to explore the intracranial efficacy of aumolertinib plus anlotinib for NSCLC with BMs, with 87 patients enrolled. Median intracranial progression-free survival (PFS) was 30.2 months, median overall PFS was 22.5 months, and median overall survival was not reached. The intracranial objective response rate and intracranial disease control rate were 71.3% and 93.1%. Patients with exon 19 deletion or wild-type TP53 exhibited significantly longer intracranial PFS and PFS compared to those with exon 21 L858R mutation or mutated TP53. Aumolertinib plus anlotinib was effective and well-tolerated as first-line therapy in EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients with BMs. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov(identifier NCT04978753, registered July 20, 2021).
Subject terms: Cancer, Oncology
Introduction
Approximately 40% to 50% of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients develop brain metastases during the course of their disease, and 10% to 25% of advanced NSCLC patients already have brain metastases at initial diagnosis1,2. Patients with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations have an even higher risk of developing brain metastases3,4. NSCLC patients with brain metastases face significant treatment challenges and have a poor prognosis. Improving the treatment outcomes for NSCLC patients with brain metastases is a critical aspect of managing EGFR-mutant NSCLC.
For advanced NSCLC patients with EGFR mutations, EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have been the standard first-line treatment5–7. Emerging evidence suggests that EGFR-TKIs can also demonstrate efficacy against intracranial lesions8–10. Osimertinib, the first globally approved third-generation EGFR-TKI, demonstrated improved intracranial objective response rate (iORR) and median intracranial progression-free survival (iPFS) in the subgroup analysis of patients with brain metastases from the FLAURA trial11. Aumolertinib is a novel oral, irreversible third-generation EGFR-TKI. It exhibits similar anti-tumor activity to osimertinib but may have a lower toxicity profile due to its optimized structure, which reduces non-selective metabolites. Aumolertinib effectively inhibits both EGFR-sensitizing mutations and the T790M resistance mutation, and demonstrates efficacy against brain metastases. Among the subgroup of patients with brain metastases, the median progression-free survival (PFS) reached 15.3 months12. While third-generation EGFR-TKIs have demonstrated improved PFS and overall survival (OS) compared to first- and second-generation EGFR-TKIs, the benefits are still transient, and disease progression is ultimately inevitable. Acquired resistance remains the primary limitation of EGFR-TKI monotherapy13. Therefore, combination treatment strategies to delay the onset of resistance and further extend survival benefits warrant exploration.
The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) pathway is essential for tumor angiogenesis in lung cancer. Dual inhibition of both the VEGF and EGFR signaling pathways may enhance the efficacy of EGFR-targeted therapies and overcome resistance to EGFR-TKIs14. Recent large-scale randomized studies, such as JO25567, NEJ026, and RELAY, have reported that the combination of anti-angiogenic agents and EGFR-TKIs can significantly improve PFS in untreated EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients15–17. However, the intravenous administration of anti-angiogenic monoclonal antibodies poses several practical challenges in clinical use. Anlotinib is a selective inhibitor of VEGFR1/2/3, FGFR1/2/3, and PDGFRα/β, and is the only effective vascular-targeted monotherapy approved for the treatment of advanced NSCLC18. FL-ALTER study demonstrated that the combination of gefitinib and anlotinib significantly improved PFS compared to gefitinib monotherapy in treatment-naïve NSCLC patients with EGFR-sensitizing mutations19. However, the efficacy and safety of the third-generation EGFR-TKIs combined with anlotinib as first-line treatment for NSCLC with brain metastases have not been reported, highlighting the urgent need for prospective studies. Herein, we present the results of a prospective, single-arm, phase 2 clinical trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of aumolertinib in combination with anlotinib in EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients with brain metastases.
Results
Patients
Between May 7, 2020, and July 25, 2024, 87 patients were enrolled and received aumolertinib plus anlotinib (flowchart of the trial in Fig. S1). Baseline characteristics were summarized in Table 1. Most patients were nonsmokers and had lung adenocarcinoma. Regarding EGFR mutation type, 46 patients (52.9%) had exon 19 deletions, and 41 (47.1%) had exon 21 L858R mutations. Two patients presented with baseline meningeal metastases. As of the data cutoff (May 10, 2025), the median follow-up duration was 24.5 months (inter-quartile range [IQR], 15.7-32.7). In addition, 29 patients were still on the study treatment.

Intracranial efficacy
At the data cutoff, 38 patients had confirmed intracranial disease progression. The median iPFS was 30.2 months (95% CI: 14.7–45.7), with 1-year and 2-year iPFS rates of 65.4% (95% CI: 55.2–77.4) and 52.2% (95% CI: 41.1–66.3), respectively (Fig. 1A). Intracranial PFS was longer in patients with exon 19 deletion compared to those with L858R mutation in exon 21 (33.2 vs 13.8 months, HR = 0.42, 95% CI: 0.22–0.81) (Fig. 2A). The iORR was 71.3% (62/87, 95% CI: 61.0–79.7), with CR in 10 patients (11.5%) and PR in 52 patients (59.8%; Table 2). The iDCR was 93.1% (95% CI: 85.8–96.8) of 87 patients. The maximum tumor change from baseline in intracranial tumors and extracranial tumors is shown in Fig. 3A. The subgroup analyses of iORR are found in Fig. S2. The iORR was 82.6% (38/46, 95% CI: 69.3–90.9) in the subgroup of exon 19 deletion and 56.1% (23/41, 95% CI: 41.0–70.1) in the subgroup of L858R mutations.

A total of 7 patients (7/14, 50%) achieved clinical benefit from treatment, with a transition from symptomatic to asymptomatic brain metastases. Among these, 6 patients with symptomatic brain metastases were receiving corticosteroid therapy at baseline; following treatment with aumolertinib plus anlotinib, all were able to discontinue corticosteroid therapy.
At disease progression, 21 patients had intracranial lesion progression only, 14 patients had extracranial lesion progression only, and 17 patients had simultaneous intracranial and extracranial lesion progression. Patients’ progressive patterns is noted in Table S1.
Of the 48 patients with iPFS < 12 months, 25 had a true intracranial progression event. The remaining 23 patients were discontinued from the study for the following reasons: 6 patients had extracranial progression only, 12 patients had < 12 months of follow-up due to late enrollment, 4 patients due to a changed protocol, and 1 patient was lost to follow-up.
Systemic efficacy
At the data cutoff, 35 patients had systemic disease progression. The median PFS was 22.5 months (95% CI: 16.5–not reached [NR]) (Fig. 1B), and the median duration of therapy was 11.0 months (IQR: 6.1–18.7) for aumolertinib and 10.3 months (IQR: 4.7–17.9) for anlotinib. Notably, 29 patients were still receiving treatment at the data cutoff, which may lead to an underestimation of the actual treatment exposure.
The overall ORR was 70.1% (61/87, 95% CI: 59.8–78.7). The PFS was longer in patients with exon 19 deletion compared to those with L858R mutation in exon 21 (34.9 vs 14.2 months, HR = 0.37, 95% CI: 0.19–0.73) (Fig. 2B). Figure 3B shows a swimming plot of the overall and intracranial objective response and duration of therapy. In addition, the figure shows the time points of notable clinical events such as confirmed intracranial progression or death. At the data cutoff, with a total of 17 deaths occurred, the median OS was not reached (Fig. 1C).
Safety analysis
Treatment-related AEs occurred in 48 (55.2%) of the 87 patients (Table S2). The treatment-related AEs of grade 3 or higher were observed in 18 patients (20.7%), the most common of which were hypertension (6 [6.9%]), diarrhea (3 [3.4%]), and thromboembolic events (3 [3.4%]). Dose reductions of anlotinib were reported in 6 patients (6.9%). Temporary treatment interruptions occurred in 4 patients (4.6%) who received anlotinib. Permanent treatment discontinuation due to AEs occurred in 11 patients (12.6%) receiving anlotinib and 1 patient (1.1%) receiving aumolertinib. No treatment-related deaths occurred.
Treatment response and concurrent mutations
A total of 68 patients (78.2%) had baseline next-generation sequencing (NGS) data available. The baseline landscape of concurrent mutations in patients is shown in Fig. S3A. The majority of the patients (72.1%, 49/68) had concurrent mutations. TP53, EGFR (other mutation or amplification), and CDKN2A (mutation or loss) were the three most frequently concurrent genes. Among patients who experienced disease progression, we noted that some exhibited responses lasting only a few months. Consequently, we further undertook clinical efficacy assessment and concurrent genomic analysis to explore potential factors influencing the efficacy of aumolertinib combined with anlotinib therapy. Patients with mutated TP53 exhibited a significantly shorter iPFS (13.8 vs 34.9 months, P = 0.015) and PFS (11.9 vs 34.9 months, P = 0.014) compared to those with wild-type TP53 (Fig. S3B, C).
Possible resistance mechanisms and postprogression treatment
A total of 13 patients underwent next-generation sequencing for resistance gene testing at the time of disease progression. This cohort included 4 patients with only intracranial progression (samples from cerebrospinal fluid), 3 patients with only extracranial progression (samples from the site of progression), and 6 patients with both intracranial and extracranial progression (of which 3 patients had CSF samples tested, and 3 patients had samples obtained from the site of extracranial progression). The results indicated that all 3 patients with progression confined to the extracranial region exhibited MET amplification (Fig. S4). These findings may suggest potential resistance mechanisms following treatment with aumolertinib in combination with anlotinib. Among the 3 patients with MET amplification, subsequent second-line therapy involving third-generation EGFR-TKIs combined with MET-targeted agents demonstrated favorable treatment outcomes, with 1 patient experiencing PFS of 18.7 months, while the other 2 patients have not yet experienced extracranial progression. In total, 35 patients received at least one subsequent treatment after disease progression, with detailed treatment information provided in Table S3. 24 patients continued to receive a second third-generation EGFR-TKI during their second-line treatment, with a PFS of 5.3 months (95% CI, 4.0–7.5) (Fig. S5).
Discussion
To our knowledge, Alot BRAIN is the first prospective trial to report the activity and safety of the third-generation EGFR-TKI combined with an anti-angiogenic agent as first-line therapy in patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC and brain metastases. Our findings indicate that this combination therapy is associated with encouraging intracranial and systemic efficacy, as evidenced by a confirmed iORR of 71.3% and a median iPFS of 30.2 months.
Previous large-scale randomized studies of first-generation EGFR-TKIs combined with anti-angiogenic therapy have reported improved PFS overall; however, the conclusions regarding the brain metastases subgroup have been inconsistent (Table S4)19–21. Currently, third-generation EGFR-TKIs have become the standard first-line treatment for advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC. However, the efficacy of combining third-generation EGFR-TKIs with anti-angiogenic therapy remains inconsistent (Table S4)22. While RAMOSE study showed that ramucirumab combined with osimertinib significantly prolonged PFS, the efficacy in the brain metastases population remains unclear23. Anlotinib is an oral multi-kinase inhibitor that inhibits tumor angiogenesis and growth by blocking VEGFR, FGFR, PDGFR, and c-Kit24. Consequently, we conducted this study to evaluate the combination of third-generation EGFR-TKIs with anlotinib in treating EGFR-mutant NSCLC with brain metastases, revealing potential benefits for patients with exon 19 deletions or without TP53 mutations.
At the initiation of our trial, the AENEAS study had not yet reported results for the brain metastases subgroup; therefore, we designed our statistical hypotheses based on data from FLAURA study11. The subgroup analysis results from FLAURA study demonstrated that osimertinib significantly improved PFS (15.2 months) and iPFS (not reached) in patients with baseline brain metastases11,25. FURLONG study reported that furmonertinib achieved superior PFS (18.0 months) and iPFS (20.8 months) compared with gefitinib in EGFR-mutated NSCLC patients with brain metastases (Table S5)26,27. The AENEAS study later reported a PFS of 15.3 months for brain metastases patients treated with aumolertinib monotherapy, and a more recent update noted a central nervous system (CNS) PFS of 29.0 months12,28. The LASER301 study also supported the robust intracranial efficacy of third-generation EGFR-TKIs, with lazertinib achieving a median iPFS of 28.2 months and median PFS of 16.4 months in patients with baseline brain metastases (Table S5)29,30. Notably, 24% of patients had received prior brain radiotherapy and 91% had 1–3 lesions, suggesting that the trial population had relatively low intracranial tumor burden at baseline, which could partially explain the favorable outcomes observed. Similarly, in our study, first-line treatment with aumolertinib plus anlotinib achieved a median PFS of 22.5 months and iPFS of 30.2 months, both numerically exceeding the PFS/iPFS reported in previous studies12,28–30. CNS penetration is known to be a key determinant of intracranial antitumor activity. Aumolertinib achieves drug concentrations in the brain at least sevenfold higher than in plasma levels, as reported in preclinical in vivo studies in rats28. Aumolertinib also showed a protective effect on the development of new CNS metastases. This is consistent with the reported CNS efficacy in AENEAS study28. These results also align with aumolertinib’s promising efficacy in the CNS in our study.
While our observed iPFS (30.2 months) appears only slightly longer, we hypothesize that the added benefit of anlotinib may be obscured by multiple factors. First, the design of the studies and sample size may have contributed to the discrepancies; the statistical limitations associated with subgroup analyses and the small sample size restrict the generalizability of the conclusions, as the aumolertinib group in the AENEAS brain metastases subgroup comprised only 28 patients. Second, the AENEAS study included a population of asymptomatic, stable patients with brain metastases, and the specific number and size of brain metastases among the enrolled patients were not known, both of which could influence the efficacy outcomes. Third, some patients had undergone radiotherapy for their brain metastases in AENEAS study. Taken together, while the numerical difference in iPFS appears small, the combination of aumolertinib with anlotinib may provide additional clinical benefits in controlling both systemic and intracranial disease progression, particularly in patients with higher baseline intracranial tumor burden or limited prior local therapy. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that due to the limited availability of prospective studies focused on brain metastases, we were only able to make a superficial comparison of our trial data with subgroup data from these large Phase III studies, which may be inappropriate. Previous studies have shown that combining EGFR-TKIs with anti-angiogenic therapies has extended PFS but has not improved OS16,19,20. Our OS data are still immature, and we anticipate future follow-up results.
The incidence of treatment-related AEs in our study was lower than that reported in AENEAS study. In our trial, treatment-related AEs of any grade and grade ≥3 were observed in 55.2% and 20.7% of patients, respectively, while the corresponding rates in AENEAS study with aumolertinib monotherapy were 98.0% and 21.6%12. Several factors may explain this discrepancy. First, differences in AE data collection and reporting methods could contribute. In our study, AE evaluation was investigator-reported and performed in a single-center setting, whereas AENEAS was a multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, likely with more rigorous AE monitoring and documentation protocols. Second, differences in patient populations and baseline characteristics may have influenced AE profiles. Our trial exclusively enrolled patients with brain metastases, many of whom were asymptomatic or received corticosteroids, potentially reducing inflammation-related toxicities. Third, co-administration of anlotinib may have led to earlier dose modifications or treatment interruptions, potentially mitigating cumulative toxicity. Despite these differences, the combination regimen demonstrated a manageable safety profile consistent with the known adverse event spectrum of each agent.
The combination of aumolertinib and anlotinib as first-line treatment for EGFR-mutant NSCLC with brain metastases demonstrated encouraging intracranial and systemic activity, potentially enhancing anti-tumor efficacy through synergistic mechanisms. Anti-angiogenic therapy can normalize abnormal tumor vasculature, enhance drug delivery, and reduce hypoxia-induced resistance mechanisms14. EGFR and VEGFR share common downstream signaling pathways, and EGFR activation has been shown to improve VEGF expression31. This forms the basis of combination therapy targeting the EGFR/VEGFR axis. Additionally, this combination may also offer a strategy to delay resistance to EGFR-TKIs. Anti-angiogenic therapy may improve the hypoxic tumor microenvironment and reduce the activation of alternative survival pathways. The normalization of blood vessels may restore the infiltration levels of cytotoxic T cells, thereby enhancing anti-tumor responses32. Furthermore, anlotinib’s inhibition of multiple tyrosine kinases may block alternative angiogenic and proliferative signals activated during EGFR-TKI resistance, thus extending the therapeutic benefit33.
Patients harboring exon 19 deletion (19del) have better efficacy and prognosis with EGFR-TKIs as first-line treatment than those of L858R mutation34,35. The AENEAS study demonstrated the median PFS for L858R group and 19del group was 13.4 months and 20.8 months, respectively12. Similarly, recent first-line combination regimens, including FLAURA2 (osimertinib plus chemotherapy) and MARIPOSA (amivantamab plus lazertinib)36,37, demonstrated favorable efficacy across both mutation subgroups, regardless of the presence of brain metastases. For example, in the FLAURA2 study, median PFS was 27.9 months and 24.7 months for patients with 19del and L858R mutations, respectively. Due to the differences in sensitivity between these two mutations, our study demonstrated that the combination of aumolertinib and anlotinib achieved significantly longer iPFS (33.2 vs. 13.8 months) and PFS (34.9 vs. 14.2 months) in the 19del subgroup, consistent with prior reports. However, compared to the previous studies12,36,37, our study demonstrated the better mPFS in the 19del group. This differential efficacy is believed to stem from several biological and structural distinctions. First, the structural differences in the EGFR kinase domain affect binding affinity, with L858R having a looser ATP-binding site, resulting in lower sensitivity to TKIs38. Second, 19del mutations are more likely to induce G1 phase arrest, whereas L858R-mutant cells exhibit a higher proportion in G2 phase, indicating incomplete cell cycle inhibition and continued proliferation39. Third, L858R mutations are more frequently accompanied by co-mutations, particularly TP53, which have been associated with resistance and poor prognosis under TKI therapy40,41. In addition, clinical characteristics may have also influenced the outcomes. A higher proportion of patients with L858R mutations presented with symptomatic brain metastases requiring treatment with mannitol and dexamethasone (Table S6), reflecting a more aggressive intracranial disease burden, potentially affecting both neurologic status and treatment tolerance. However, as this study was a single-arm trial, it cannot directly demonstrate an additive benefit of anlotinib compared to aumolertinib monotherapy or other newly approved first-line regimens. Further controlled studies are warranted to clarify whether this combination provides clinically meaningful advantages over existing standard therapies.
The role of TP53 mutations in modulating response to anti-angiogenic therapy remains controversial. While some studies have associated TP53 mutations with elevated VEGF expression and improved outcomes with anti-angiogenic agents, others have reported no significant impact42–44. This discrepancy may be attributable to variations in the types of TP53 mutations20,44. However, our study findings indicate that TP53 mutations influence the efficacy of aumolertinib combined with anlotinib in treating EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients with brain metastases. For patients with coexisting TP53 and EGFR mutations, it may be necessary to explore alternative combination treatment strategies targeting TP53.
This trial has some limitations. First, this was a single-arm, phase 2 trial and lacked a control arm, which limits the ability to adequately demonstrate the superiority of combination therapy with aumolertinib and anlotinib over monotherapy; additionally, selection bias was potentially present. Second, the follow-up was insufficient, resulting in immature survival results at the data cutoff. Third, the efficacy of aumolertinib plus anlotinib was assessed only by investigator assessment without an independent review assessment. Fourth, we did not conduct a centralized review of the detection of actionable mutations in the baseline patient characteristics. Besides, only 13 patients underwent resistance gene testing, limiting the interpretative value of the resistance mechanisms.
In conclusion, the combination of aumolertinib and anlotinib as first-line therapy displayed activity and a well-tolerated safety profile in advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients with brain metastases. Our findings provide preliminary evidence for the clinical application of this combination in patients with brain metastases from lung cancer.
Methods
Study design and participants
This was a prospective, single-arm, phase 2 clinical trial (Alot BRAIN) performed at the Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center in China. This trial was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (identifying number: NCT04978753) with the registration date of July 20, 2021. The main eligibility criteria included histologically or cytologically confirmed NSCLC with EGFR-sensitive mutation (exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R mutation); at least 3 metastatic lesions in the brain (patients with 1 to 2 lesions were also allowed if local therapy was refused or not suitable, including surgery or radiotherapy) confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); at least 1 measurable brain lesion (at least 5 mm in diameter) according to the modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors version 1.1 (modified RECIST 1.1, a criterion that allows up to 5 intracranial target lesions with 5 mm or larger in maximum diameter); asymptomatic brain metastases or with controlled symptoms of intracranial hypertension after osmotic antiedema agent (Mannitol) and steroids (dexamethasone); treatment naïve; aged 18–75 years; and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 to 2. The main exclusion criteria were mixed NSCLC and SCLC; brain lesions with active bleeding; previously receiving treatment with angiogenesis inhibitors; history of hemoptysis (more than 50 ml per day) occurring within 3 months before enrollment; and severe or uncontrolled hypertension. The full list of inclusion and exclusion criteria is available in the protocol.
The study was performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice. The study protocol was approved by the ethics committee of the Guangdong Association Study of Thoracic Oncology (ID: GASTO-1063) on May 5, 2020. Written informed consent was obtained from each patient.
Procedures
Eligible patients were orally administered combined therapy of aumolertinib (110 mg per day) and anlotinib (12 mg for BSA ≥ 1.6 m2, 10 mg for BSA < 1.6 m2, daily on days 1–14, every 3 weeks) till progression, intolerable toxicity, or death. Dose modifications of anlotinib were allowed according to the protocol-defined dose modification criteria. Dose adjustments of aumolertinib were performed only when patients experienced adverse events (AEs) related to EGFR-TKIs. Details for dose reduction, interruption, and AE management are available in the protocol.
Tumors were assessed by the study investigators every 3 cycles after study initiation using contrast-enhanced MRI according to modified RECIST 1.1 for intracranial lesions or computed tomography (CT) according to RECIST 1.1 for extracranial lesions. Follow-up for survival was done every 3 months after treatment discontinuation. AEs were monitored continuously until 90 days after the last dose and were graded according to National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.03.
Outcomes
The primary endpoint was iPFS, defined as the time from the date of enrollment (the initiation of initial treatment) to intracranial disease progression or death. The secondary end points included PFS, defined as the time from the date of enrollment to overall disease (both intracranial and extracranial) progression or death; OS, defined as the time from the date of enrollment to death from any cause; iORR, defined as the proportion of patients with complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) of intracranial lesions; intracranial disease control rate (iDCR), defined as the proportion of patients with CR or PR or stable disease (SD) of intracranial lesions; and safety. Duration of therapy was defined as the time from treatment initiation to permanent discontinuation of aumolertinib or anlotinib for any reason, including disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, treatment switch, loss to follow-up, or data cutoff, whichever occurred first. Clinical benefits were also assessed by the treating physician based on improvements in neurological symptoms (e.g., headache, nausea/vomiting, focal neurological deficits) following treatment initiation, and documented in the medical records.
Statistical analysis
Referring to previous studies and data for similar agents11, the median PFS of the third-generation EGFR-TKI in the first-line treatment of EGFR-positive NSCLC with brain metastases was estimated at 15.2 months. We hypothesized that median iPFS be prolonged from 15.2 months to 23 months, with 80% power, a 1-sided significance level of 10%, and a 10% dropout rate; therefore, our estimated sample size was 87 patients.
The statistical analysis plan was pre-specified before patient enrollment. All efficacy analyses were conducted in the intention-to-treat population, defined as all enrolled patients who received at least one dose of study treatment. Safety analyses were conducted in all patients who received at least one dose of aumolertinib or anlotinib and had at least one post-baseline safety evaluation.
Intracranial PFS, PFS, and OS were estimated using Kaplan-Meier curves, and differences between groups were compared with a stratified log-rank test. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs were evaluated with Cox proportional hazards regression models. Patients without intracranial progression or death were censored at the date of the last adequate intracranial tumor assessment (for iPFS). Patients without documented progression or death were censored at the last tumor assessment date (for PFS) or last known alive date (for OS). Intracranial ORR and intracranial DCR were calculated with 95% CIs by the Clopper-Pearson method. Pre-specified subgroup analyses were performed based on patients’ baseline characteristics (e.g., EGFR mutation subtype, TP53 mutation status). In addition, a post-hoc exploratory analysis was performed to evaluate clinical benefit, as defined in the Outcomes section.
No formal adjustment for multiplicity was performed, as this was a single-arm phase 2 study with a hypothesis-generating intent. All endpoints were reported as 2-sided P-values in this study, with a significance threshold of 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using R software, version 4.4.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing).
